Issued at 213 PM CDT Wed Jul 22 2026

**UNSEASONABLY COOL WEATHER & LIGHT RAIN CHANCES (Through 
Friday night)**

Today, a 1020 mb sfc anticyclone continues to slide in from the
northwest, bringing cooler & drier air, lighter surface winds, 
and mainly clear skies (with the exception of some diurnal cu 
and thin cirrus). Daily high temperatures in the mid-upper 70s 
(8-10 degrees below normal for this time of year) and morning 
lows in the mid-upper 50s will persist through Friday. Dewpoints
remaining in the 50s will also make for comfortable humidity 
levels. This high pressure system will dominate the Midwest and 
Lower Great Lakes region before translating east into the Mid- 
Atlantic by the weekend. 

A mid-level shortwave traversing the central Plains on Friday 
will promote forcing for a broad shield of rain showers 
extending into the mid-Mississippi River Valley through the 
evening. Given PWATs of 2 inches clipping the southwest portion 
of the CWA, WPC has introduced a marginal (5-15%) chance of 
excessive rainfall, mainly south and west of a Beardstown to 
Shelbyville line, where PoPs are highest (30-50% range) late 
Friday. Forecast soundings suggest the low-level air mass will 
remain dry enough for much of this activity to become virga, 
though enough top-down saturation will likely occur for some 
showers to produce rainfall. The ECMWF suite has been an outlier
in depicting a further northeast track of the disturbance, 
resulting in more notable rainfall amounts across the area. For 
now, NBM has up to one-quarter inch of rain in our southwestern 
counties.

**DANGEROUS HEAT (Sunday and Monday)**

As the sfc ridge pushes east of Illinois by the early weekend, 
southerly low-level flow will return, prompting the transport of
warmer temperatures and higher dewpoints back into the area. 
Seasonable temps and humidity on Saturday quickly transition 
into dangerous heat by Sunday. Afternoon highs in the low-to-mid
90s combined with dewpoints in the mid-70s will push heat 
indices into the 105-110 degree range in some locations, 
especially west of I-55, where LREF probabilities of reaching 
heat advisory criteria are 30-40%. Nighttime lows look to only 
dip into the mid-to-upper 70s, offering little relief through 
Tuesday AM. However, cannot rule out any scattered storm 
clusters putting a damper in peak heating for some areas on both
days, though the location and timing of this is difficult to 
outline at this range.

**STORM CHANCES RETURN...SOME STRONG-TO-SEVERE (Sunday through
Tuesday)**

The poleward advection of rich Gulf moisture through the 
weekend will begin to introduce plentiful fuel (MLCAPE up to 
3000-4000 J/kg) for thunderstorms back to the Midwest. A rather 
persistent synoptic pattern, consisting of a mid-level ridge 
centered near the Front Range, and a longwave trough from 
Ontario into the East Coast, places the region under a 45-65 kt 
belt of northwesterly mid-level flow through next week. 
Resulting 0-6 km bulk shear of 30-45 kts will be favorable for 
the organization of any storms that occur. Forcing is nebulous 
on Saturday, given the jet core is positioned well north and 
there are no notable embedded shortwaves to speak of in the 
area. Still, cannot rule out an isolated storm, mainly towards 
northern IL. The main focus shifts to Sunday through Tuesday, as
a series of convectively-augmented shortwaves may traverse the 
ridge and provide enough forcing for strong-to-severe 
thunderstorm clusters in the Midwest, some of which may have the
tendency to dive southward into our area. PWATs of 1.8-2.0 
inches and any training storms may yield localized flooding as 
well. The extent and evolution of this activity will depend upon
how upstream convection plays out each preceding day.

Though the SPC does not yet have any severe weather outlines 
for this period, extended-range ML guidance is consistent in 
highlighting central Illinois in daily 5-15% chances for severe 
thunderstorms. At this range, uncertainty is too high in exact 
placement and timing, so will have to monitor how forcing 
mechanisms iron out in the guidance in the coming days.

**PLEASANT WEATHER (Middle of next week)**

During the early-middle part of next week, a stronger cold 
front is likely to sweep through the area, ushering in pleasant 
weather and high pressure thereafter. Models are in some 
disagreement on the timing of this frontal passage, given the 
series of mid-level waves traversing the ridge, though FROPA 
should be on Tuesday. If the front ends up faster than depicted,
the aforementioned chance of strong storms on Tuesday could be 
shunted south of the CWA.
